extracted.intended_audience: trade lawyers, tribunal members, government officials, and legal scholars working on anti-dumping and countervailing proceedings (particularly in Canada)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria governing the Anti-dumping Tribunal's powers, procedure, and substantive tests (material injury, causation, indicators, confidentiality, timing, and related regulatory computations) used in Canadian anti-dumping and countervailing investigations and determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Tribunal inquiry under section 16(1)(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt of a notice of a preliminary determination from the Deputy Minister, the Tribunal shall make inquiry as to whether the dumping has caused (or would have caused in the absence of provisional duty), is causing or is likely to cause material injury to the production of like goods, or has materially retarded or is materially retarding the establishment of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core statutory mandate for most Tribunal proceedings (the majority of findings are under s.16). The inquiry focuses on past, present and likely future injury to production of like goods. Statements of reasons typically recite the preliminary determination, procedural details, identify the product and Canadian industry, examine claims of material injury, and conclude whether injury exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry re: 'considerable importation' and importer awareness (section 16(1)(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunal must inquire whether, for goods to which a preliminary determination applies, there has occurred a 'considerable importation' of dumped like goods that has caused material injury, or whether the importer was or should have been aware that dumping causing injury was taking place, and whether duty should be assessed to prevent recurrence of material injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This focuses attention not just on exporter conduct but on import volumes and importers' culpability or knowledge; it can lead to assessment of duties to prevent recurrence of injury. Consideration may include import volumes, timing, and whether importer could/should have known of dumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal's power to direct further investigation (subsection 16(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal may direct the Deputy Minister to investigate the dumping of goods similar to those that are the subject of a Tribunal inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful where Tribunal needs further factual development about related goods or market segments before making findings. This is a tool for expanding or deepening the factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for Tribunal findings (section 16(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal has 90 days to make an order or finding under section 16.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory deadline for concluding inquiries under s.16; procedural scheduling must respect this limit unless statute provides otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: s.16.1 referral inquiries to Governor in Council
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 16.1 requires the Tribunal to inquire into and report to the Governor in Council on any 'matter or thing in relation to the importation of goods into Canada that may cause or threaten injury' referred by the Governor in Council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for matters referred for broader policy or investigatory reports beyond individual preliminary determinations. The Tribunal's mandate on referrals is to investigate potential or threatened injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deputy Minister's duties following Tribunal order (sections 17 and 18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsections 17(1)-(3) require the Deputy Minister to make a final determination following receipt of a Tribunal order or finding, assess the duty payable, or return any provisional duty or security to the importer; section 18 deals with goods entered subsequent to Tribunal order and appraisal of normal value and export price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The administrative follow-through after a Tribunal finding: final duties and appraisals rest with the Deputy Minister, and there are appeal pathways from these determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals from administrative determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals from the Deputy Minister's final determination or reappraisal go to the Tariff Board, and then questions of law may be appealed to the Federal Court of Canada.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out the review route for parties dissatisfied with administrative or appraisal decisions; distinction between factual/appraisal determinations and questions of law is important for litigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal composition and rulemaking powers (Part III / s.21, s.23, s.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal consists of not more than five members appointed for seven years, with a Chairman and Vice-Chairman; the Chairman is chief executive officer responsible for work assignment; the Tribunal may, with Governor in Council approval, make procedural rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational/administrative features explain authority to adopt procedural rules (e.g., 1974 Rules) and internal allocation of hearings and duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal as a 'court of record' and attendant powers (subsection 27(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal has, regarding attendance, swearing and examination of witnesses, production and inspection of documents, enforcement of orders, entry upon and inspection of property, and other matters necessary for due exercise of its jurisdiction, all such powers, rights and privileges as are vested in a superior court of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This designation has encouraged formality and has been a focus of judicial scrutiny of Tribunal procedures. It supports evidentiary powers and enforcement mechanisms similar to courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential business information protections (subsection 29(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where evidence or information that is in its nature confidential, relating to the business or affairs of any person, firm or corporation, is given or elicited in the course of any inquiry under section 16, the evidence or information shall not be made public in such a manner as to be available for the use of any business competitor or rival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal must balance disclosure to parties with protection of confidential commercial information; subsection 29(3) frames how confidential material should be treated — not disclosed publicly in a way that benefits competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of parties to appear and representation; public or in camera hearings (section 29)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties to a hearing may appear in person, or by counsel or agent, and a hearing may be heard in camera, or in public at the discretion of the Tribunal or Chairman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory right to appear and be represented underpins natural justice protections; tribunal may exercise discretion on public vs closed sessions, consistent with confidentiality rules and fair hearing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to review, rescind, alter or rehear orders (section 31)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal, after any order or finding, may review, rescind, change or alter the order or finding, or re-hear any matter before deciding it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides flexibility for correcting or revisiting decisions; historical changes removed prior privative clauses that restricted judicial review elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory rules for determining normal value and export price (various regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations deal with selection of sales at appropriate trade level and comparable quantities (Regulation 3); adjustments of normal value for quantity discounts (4), differences in quality/structure/design/material (5), deferred discounts/cash discounts (6-7), costs of transportation (8); other computation issues including trade level adjustments (10), rebates/ duty drawbacks (11), exchange rates (12), computation period (14), goods in transit through third countries, costs of export (18) and compensatory arrangements (19A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations are focused on methodological rules for valuing normal value and export price; they provide detailed adjustment rules used in determining dumping margins. These technical rules are distinct from injury analysis but are central to establishing dumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countervailing duty initiation and Tribunal referral procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Deputy Minister shall initiate an investigation respecting subsidization of imported goods when there is evidence of subsidization and prima facie evidence of material injury; Deputy Minister may make a preliminary determination of subsidization, notify Ministers, and the Minister of National Revenue (with concurrence of Minister of Finance) applies to Governor in Council for provisional countervailing duty and for a reference under section 16.1 to the Tribunal to determine whether subsidized importation has caused or is likely to cause material injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel procedure to anti-dumping: preliminary findings, provisional duties, and Tribunal referral for injury inquiry; if Tribunal finds injury, application for countervailing duty equal to subsidy amount follows; if no injury, provisional duties are returned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of fair hearing and disclosure of evidence (Magnasonic / Sarco jurisprudence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties have a statutory right to appear at hearings which implies a right to be heard, including a fair opportunity to answer anything adverse to their interest and to make submissions regarding material the Tribunal proposes to base its decision on; the Tribunal must not act on material not put before parties or accept information in a manner depriving parties of the chance to test it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnasonic held that the Tribunal acted on information not put before parties and denied opportunity to answer — decision accordingly quashed. Sarco reaffirmed the need to give interested parties a full and fair opportunity to be heard. Anti-pattern: receiving confidential evidence or outside visits without providing parties opportunity to know and respond to that evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of material injury (Article 3(b) style list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of injury should be based on factors such as turnover, market share, profits, the price of the dumped goods compared to the price of domestically produced goods, export performance, employment, volume of dumped and other imports, utilization of capacity, productivity, and restrictive trade practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Canadian Act/regulations do not specify injury indicators, Tribunal practice has adopted these quantitative and qualitative indicators. They provide the empirical basis for assessing whether material injury exists but require interpretation (see separate rubric on interpretive issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional injury factors to consider (Article 3(c) style list)
rubrics_metrics.description: In establishing injury, attention must be paid to factors such as volume and prices of undumped imports, competition between domestic producers, and contraction in demand due to substitution of other products or changes in consumer taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 3(c) emphasizes that injury assessment must consider alternative explanations and market dynamics; failure to do so risks misattributing injury to dumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule II mandated briefing items (1974 Rules of Procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefs, written submissions and evidence must contain information relating to: (a) retardation in the implementation of definite plans for production; (b) loss of orders, markets and profits; (c) reduced employment; (d) reduced utilization of capacity by producers in Canada of like goods; (e) the volume of imported goods that are dumped, where known; and (f) the price erosion resulting from the dumping of the goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule II formalizes many of the Tribunal's material-injury indicators and requires parties to present evidence on these points. Although inventories, distribution costs and R&D curtailment are not listed, the Tribunal continues to consider them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonly considered supplementary indicators (inventories, distribution costs, R&D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not listed in Rule II, the Tribunal continues to consider unusually high inventories, higher unit distribution costs, and curtailment of research and development as indicators of material injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal practice extends beyond the formal list to capture broader signs of industry distress — parties should address these areas even if not expressly required by Rule II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive issues and definitional questions for indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Key interpretive questions arise (e.g., what constitutes 'capacity' — the Tribunal has said potential use of capacity is related to Canadian market requirements and not total capacity; how to assess profitability when Canadian producer is also an importer; whether 'production' includes assembly of imported parts or mere repacking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators require careful definition in factual context; Tribunal precedents show fine-grained distinctions (assembly can be 'production' if substantial steps are involved; repacking for marketing convenience is not 'production'). Parties should define and support their measures and explain relevance to Canadian market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation standard: dumping must be the cause of injury (Article 3(a) principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dumping and material injury are necessary but not sufficient; dumping must be the cause of injury. Article 3(a) requires that dumped imports be 'demonstrably the principal cause of material injury' and that determinations be based on positive findings rather than mere allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal must examine all other factors that may adversely affect the industry. The causal link must be established with positive findings; mere contemporaneous correlations are insufficient without connecting evidence (e.g., underselling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary approaches and cautions on establishing causality
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmed approaches range from inferring injury from dumping to requiring evidence of underselling; some Tribunal reasoning simply equated contemporaneous increases in dumped imports with displacement of domestic sales, while more recent decisions seek a relationship between quantitative indicators and dumping (e.g., underselling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: assuming causality by correlation alone or shifting the burden unfairly to exporters/importers (negative test). Preferred practice is to examine alternative explanations, seek underselling evidence, and build a reasoned, positive finding linking dumping to injury. The Tribunal has criticized reasoning that relies on ad hoc inferences without establishing a causal relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to examine 'other factors' and alternatives to dumping
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering injury, all other factors which, individually or in combination, may be adversely affecting the industry (e.g., recession, market saturation, competition among domestic producers, failure to keep abreast of product development, wage levels, higher input costs, limited market size) shall be examined to decide whether they alone explain injury or have only increased susceptibility to injury from dumping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal practice sometimes failed to fully explain other factors in reasons; robust analysis should identify and weigh these factors, and assess whether they are the primary cause or merely exacerbating conditions that make the industry more vulnerable to dumped imports.
